Prealgebra · Lesson 2.4

Negative Powers

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Every power you have met so far makes a number bigger. Exponents do not have to stop at zero, though. Each step down the ladder divides by the base, and that pattern keeps right on going below zero. This section is about the powers you find down there.

Problem
A glacier lab logs ice thickness in powers of 5 centimetres. Reading down the column the entries are 53=12553=125, 52=2552=25, 51=551=5, and each step down divides the thickness by 5. The next entry is 5050. What number is 5050?
Show a hint
  • Take the entry above, 51=551=5, and divide it by 5 the way every step down does.
  • Dividing 5 by 5 leaves a single value, and it matches the rule that any nonzero base to the zero power gives the same number.
Show the full solution
Each step down divides by 5. From 51=551=5, one more step gives 5÷5=15÷5=1, so 50=150=1​. The zero power sits exactly where the dividing-by-5 pattern says it should.
Problem
Keep going down the same column. Below 50=150=1 the lab writes 5−15−1, still made by dividing the entry above it by 5. What number is 5−15−1? Write it as a fraction.
Show a hint
  • The entry above is 50=150=1. Divide it by 5 like every other step.
  • Dividing 1 by 5 gives a fraction smaller than 1. The exponent went negative and so the number dropped below 1.
Show the full solution
One more step down divides 50=150=1 by 5, giving 1÷5=151÷5=51​. So 5−1=155−1=51​​. A negative exponent has flipped the base into the bottom of a fraction.

There is a second way to see the same fact, using the quotient rule you already know. Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents. When the bottom exponent is the larger one, that subtraction gives a negative number.

Problem
A delivery drone climbs in stages, each multiplying its altitude by 4. Compute 42454542​ two ways. First as a plain fraction by writing out the factors and cancelling, then by the quotient rule which subtracts 2−52−5. What negative power of 4 do both ways give? Give the exponent only.
Show a hint
  • Cancelling two 4s from top and bottom leaves three 4s in the denominator, so the fraction is 143431​.
  • The quotient rule says 42−5=4−342−5=4−3, and that must equal the 143431​ you found. The exponent is the value you read off.
Show the full solution
Writing the factors, two 4s cancel and three remain underneath, so 4245=1434542​=431​. The quotient rule agrees, 42−5=4−342−5=4−3. The two views match, 4−3=1434−3=431​, and the exponent is −3−3​.
Problem
A pollen grain seen under a microscope has width 3−43−4 of a millimetre. Write 3−43−4 as a single fraction.
Show a hint
  • A negative exponent puts the matching positive power in the denominator.
  • So this is 134341​, and 34=8134=81.
Show the full solution
Flip the base under the bar with its matching positive power. 3−4=134=1813−4=341​=811​ So the width is 181811​​ of a millimetre.
Key idea
A nonzero base raised to a negative exponent equals 11 over that base raised to the matching positive power, a−n=1ana−n=an1​ (for a≠0a=0). List the powers in decreasing order. Each step down divides by the base, and dividing past a0=1a0=1 moves the base below the fraction bar. The quotient rule gives the same result, aman=am−nanam​=am−n. When the bottom exponent is larger, the leftover factors stay in the denominator.

A negative exponent means a reciprocal, and that single idea also runs in reverse. If the base is already a fraction, a negative exponent flips it back up. The next two problems push on that.

Problem
A zoom lens reverses its setting. The reduced view was 1441​, and reversing it raises that to the power −3−3. Evaluate (14)−3(41​)−3 as a whole number.
Show a hint
  • A negative exponent takes the reciprocal of the base. The reciprocal of 1441​ is 4.
  • So (14)−3=43(41​)−3=43. Now cube 4.
Show the full solution
A negative exponent flips the base over, and the reciprocal of 1441​ is 4. (14)−3=43=64(41​)−3=43=64 So the value is 6464​. A fraction raised to a negative power turns upright and grows.
Problem
A relay stores the reciprocal of 5 as 5−15−1, then a reset raises that stored value to the power −2−2. Evaluate (5−1)−2(5−1)−2 as a whole number.
Show a hint
  • A power to a power multiplies the exponents, (−1)×(−2)(−1)×(−2), or read 5−15−1 as the reciprocal 1551​ and flip it back up.
  • Either way you land on 5252. Now square 5.
Show the full solution
A power to a power multiplies the exponents, and (−1)×(−2)=2(−1)×(−2)=2. (5−1)−2=5(−1)×(−2)=52=25(5−1)−2=5(−1)×(−2)=52=25 The value is 2525​. Two flips undo each other, so the reciprocal comes back upright.
Key idea
A fraction raised to a negative power becomes its reciprocal with a positive exponent. A reciprocal in the base means the same as a minus sign in the exponent, so (1a)n=a−n(a1​)n=a−n and (a−1)n=a−n(a−1)n=a−n. Moving a power from one side of the fraction bar to the other changes the sign of its exponent.
Fun fact
Scientists lean on negative powers of ten constantly. A nanometre is 10−910−9 of a metre, the rough width of a few atoms side by side, and a picosecond is 10−1210−12 of a second. Light travels less than a millimetre in one of those. The same negative exponents that shrink fractions also name the smallest things people have ever measured.

Here is where negative powers become genuinely useful. Once exponents can go negative, the product and quotient rules work across zero without any new rules. Adding exponents is just adding numbers, and some of those numbers are now below zero.

Problem
A cipher key is built as 76×7−476×7−4. Use the product rule to combine it into a single power of 7, then give that power's value.
Show a hint
  • Adding the exponents is allowed even when one is negative. Add 66 and −4−4.
  • 6+(−4)=26+(−4)=2, so the key is 7272.
Show the full solution
Add the exponents. 76×7−4=76+(−4)=72=4976×7−4=76+(−4)=72=49 The value is 4949​. Adding a negative exponent is the same as subtracting, so the product rule works straight across zero.
Problem
A camera meter sets two opposing exposure stops that multiply to 95×9−595×9−5. Combine them into a single power of 9 and give its value.
Show a hint
  • Add the exponents, 5+(−5)5+(−5).
  • The exponents cancel to zero, and any nonzero base to the zero power gives the same number.
Show the full solution
The exponents are opposites and add to zero. 95×9−5=95+(−5)=90=195×9−5=95+(−5)=90=1 A power times its reciprocal collapses to 11​.
Problem
A spinning rotor multiplies its energy by 4 each round. After one round the energy is 4141 units, but the formula divides by the rotor's idle reading 4−34−3, giving 414−34−341​. Write the result as a single power of 4 and give its value.
Show a hint
  • Dividing by 4−34−3 subtracts that exponent, 1−(−3)1−(−3). Subtracting a negative adds.
  • 1−(−3)=41−(−3)=4, so the result is 4444.
Show the full solution
The quotient rule subtracts the bottom exponent. 414−3=41−(−3)=44=2564−341​=41−(−3)=44=256 The value is 256256​. Subtracting a negative adds, so dividing by a negative power raises the exponent.
Key idea
Every law of exponents keeps working once the exponents go negative. Multiplying same-base powers still adds the exponents, dividing still subtracts them, and a power of a power still multiplies them. In symbols, am×a−n=am−nam×a−n=am−n and ama−n=am+na−nam​=am+n.

Negative bases and negative exponents can show up together, and then the parentheses decide the sign. The next problem lines up three expressions that look almost the same, and only one of them is positive. Check what each exponent applies to and what each minus sign covers.

Problem
Exactly one of these three is a positive number. −2−4,(−5)−2,(−2)−3−2−4,(−5)−2,(−2)−3 Find the one that is positive and give its value as a fraction.
Show a hint
  • In −2−4−2−4 the exponent grips only the 2 and the minus waits outside, so it is −116−161​, a negative. In (−5)−2(−5)−2 the parentheses trap the sign and an even power makes it positive.
  • In (−2)−3(−2)−3 the sign is inside but an odd power keeps it negative, −18−81​. That leaves (−5)−2(−5)−2 as the only positive, so evaluate 1(−5)2(−5)21​.
Show the full solution
(−5)−2(−5)−2 is the positive one. The parentheses hold the sign inside, and an even power of a negative is positive, so (−5)−2=1(−5)2=125(−5)−2=(−5)21​=251​​. The other two miss for different reasons. In −2−4−2−4 the exponent touches only the 2, leaving −116−161​, and in (−2)−3(−2)−3 the sign is inside but an odd power keeps it negative at −18−81​.
Key idea
With negative exponents the parentheses decide the answer. In −a−n−a−n the exponent applies only to the base and the minus sign stays outside, so the value is −1an−an1​, a negative. In (−a)−n(−a)−n the parentheses put the sign inside the base, so an even power is positive and an odd power is negative.

Letters behave exactly like numbers here. The same exponent laws combine variable powers across zero and into the negatives. The last two problems put everything from this section together.

Problem
A growth model uses the expression t3×t−7t3×t−7. Simplify it to a single power of tt, written with one exponent. Give the exponent.
Show a hint
  • The product rule adds the exponents even when they are mixed in sign. Add 33 and −7−7.
  • 3+(−7)=−43+(−7)=−4, so the result is t−4t−4. The exponent is what you read off.
Show the full solution
Add the exponents, sign and all. t3×t−7=t3+(−7)=t−4t3×t−7=t3+(−7)=t−4 The exponent is −4−4​. Written without a negative, that is 1t4t41​.
Problem
Four dials each set a magnification, all powers of 3. They read 9−3,(127)2,(13)−5,(32)−4.9−3,(271​)2,(31​)−5,(32)−4. Rewrite each as a single power of 3, then say which dial gives the smallest magnification. Give that dial's value as a power of 3, for example in the form 3^7.
Show a hint
  • Send each to base 3. A fraction to a negative power flips upright, a fraction to a positive power keeps the base downstairs, and a power to a power multiplies the exponents.
  • You should get 3−63−6, 3−63−6, 3535, and 3−83−8. With one base, the smallest exponent loses.
Show the full solution
Send every dial to base 3. 9−3=(32)−3=3−69−3=(32)−3=3−6, (127)2=27−2=(33)−2=3−6(271​)2=27−2=(33)−2=3−6, (13)−5=35(31​)−5=35, and (32)−4=32×(−4)=3−8(32)−4=32×(−4)=3−8. With one base the smallest exponent gives the smallest magnification, and the smallest of −6,−6,5,−8−6,−6,5,−8 is −8−8, so the answer is 3−83−8​, which equals 1656165611​.

Practice these ideas

Practice
You already know the exponent ladder climbs by multiplying, and that any nonzero base raised to the zero power lands on 11. The questions below walk that same ladder the other way, below zero, where each step still divides by the base. Once you see what a negative exponent really asks for, a whole shelf of reciprocal tricks opens up.
Practice
A scientist photographs a snowflake at a magnification of 5252. To study a real raindrop instead, she wants the opposite, a view shrunk by that same factor, which she writes as 5−25−2. Continue her ladder by hand. Starting from 52=2552=25, each step down divides by 55, so 51=551=5 and then 50=150=1. Take two more steps down and give the value of 5−25−2 as a fraction.
Show the solution
Each step down the ladder divides by 55. 52=25,51=5,50=1,5−1=15,5−2=12552=25,51=5,50=1,5−1=51​,5−2=251​​ The values keep shrinking by the same factor past zero, which is why 5−25−2 is the same as 152521​.
Practice
The ladder never breaks at zero. For any nonzero base bb, one more step down from b0=1b0=1 keeps dividing, so a negative exponent means a reciprocal. b−n=1bnb−n=bn1​ Read b−nb−n as one over bb raised to the matching positive power.
Practice
A relay tower's signal fades by a factor of 22 every kilometer. At the tower the strength reads 2323 units. A listener sits far enough away that the strength has fallen to 2−42−4 units. Written as a single fraction, how strong is the signal where the listener sits?
Show the solution
A negative exponent sends the power to the denominator. 2−4=124=1162−4=241​=161​​ The 2323 at the start was never needed, it only sets the scene.
Practice
A jeweler grades polishing grit by powers of 77, where a finer grit carries a smaller number. The finest cloth on the bench is labeled 7−37−3. Rewrite that label with a positive exponent only, then give its value as a fraction.
Show the solution
7−37−3 is 1 over the matching positive power, so with a positive exponent the label reads 173731​. 7−3=173=13437−3=731​=3431​​
Practice
Two filters sit in a beam of light. The first passes 4242 of every batch through, the second passes 4−54−5 of whatever reaches it. Multiply the two factors and write the combined factor as a single power of 44.
Show the solution
Same base, so multiplying adds the exponents and the minus sign rides along. 42×4−5=42+(−5)=4−342×4−5=42+(−5)=4−3​ The law that added exponents above zero keeps working straight across zero and into the negatives.
Practice
Every law of exponents you have met still holds when an exponent goes negative. Adding exponents, subtracting them, and multiplying them all carry the minus sign along without complaint. A negative exponent is a fully grown number on the ladder, not a special case.
Practice
A timekeeper records a tiny span as 102106106102​ of a day. Use the quotient rule to write this as a single power of 1010, then say how many places after the decimal point its leading digit sits.
Show the solution
Subtract the exponents, bottom from top. 102106=102−6=10−4106102​=102−6=10−4 That value is 1104=0.00011041​=0.0001, so the leading 11 sits in the 44​th place after the decimal point. The quotient rule lands you below zero whenever the bottom exponent is the larger one.
Practice
This is exactly how scientists write down extremely small numbers. A nanometer is 10−910−9 of a meter, and a single water molecule is only a few of them across. The minus sign matters here, it counts how many times you divided by ten to shrink a meter down to something you could never see.
Practice
A clockmaker winds a spring 66 full turns, recorded as 9696, then unwinds it 66 turns, recorded as 9−69−6. Combine the two as a single power of 99 and give the resulting value.
Show the solution
Same base, so add the exponents. 96×9−6=96+(−6)=90=196×9−6=96+(−6)=90=1​ A power times its opposite lands back on 90=190=1, so the spring ends where it began.
Practice
A photographer halves the light at each click of a dial. One full sweep dims the light to (12)5(21​)5 of the start. Her assistant insists the same dimming can be written as 2−52−5. Show they agree by giving the single fraction both equal.
Show the solution
Distribute the exponent over the fraction. (12)5=1525=125=2−5=132(21​)5=2515​=251​=2−5=321​ Both ways of writing it give 132321​​. Raising a reciprocal to the nn is the same thing as raising the base to the −n−n.
Practice
Flipping the base undoes the negative sign on an exponent. (1b)n=b−nand(b−1)n=b−n(b1​)n=b−nand(b−1)n=b−n A reciprocal in the base and a minus in the exponent are two names for the same flip.
Practice
A vault dial is calibrated so that the setting 88−38−38​ opens it. Simplify that to a single power of 88 and give its exponent.
Show the solution
Write the top as 8181 and subtract the bottom exponent. 88−3=818−3=81−(−3)=848−38​=8−381​=81−(−3)=84 So the exponent is 44​. Subtracting a negative adds, so dividing by a negative power raises the exponent.
Practice
In a program, a variable holds x6x6 and gets multiplied by x−2x−2, then the result is multiplied once more by x−1x−1. Write the final expression as a single power of xx.
Show the solution
All one base, so the exponents simply add. x6×x−2×x−1=x6+(−2)+(−1)=x6−3=x3x6×x−2×x−1=x6+(−2)+(−1)=x6−3=x3​ The negative exponents pull the total down without changing how the rule works.
Practice
Musicians live on this ladder without naming it. Drop an octave and a note's frequency is halved, which is one step of 2−12−1. Drop another and you are at 2−22−2. The lowest pipe on a giant organ is many such steps below middle ground, a stack of reciprocals you can feel in your chest more than hear.
Practice
A careless student claims −2−4−2−4 and (−2)−4(−2)−4 are equal. Work out each value exactly, then state the distance between them on the number line.
Show the solution
Both values are reciprocals, but the parentheses change the sign. In −2−4−2−4 the power touches only the 22, so −2−4=−124=−116.−2−4=−241​=−161​. In (−2)−4(−2)−4 the sign stays inside, and a negative base to an even power comes out positive, so (−2)−4=1(−2)4=116.(−2)−4=(−2)41​=161​. They sit on opposite sides of zero, so the distance is 116+116=216=18.161​+161​=162​=81​​. The exponent grips exactly what it touches, even when it is negative.
Practice
Three lenses are labeled by how much they enlarge an image. Lens A is (18)−5(81​)−5, lens B is (14)−7(41​)−7, and lens C is 163163. Rewrite all three as powers of 22 and name the single strongest lens.
Show the solution
Flip each reciprocal base, then send everything to base 22. (18)−5=85=(23)5=215(81​)−5=85=(23)5=215 (14)−7=47=(22)7=214(41​)−7=47=(22)7=214 163=(24)3=212163=(24)3=212 With one base the largest exponent wins, and 15>14>1215>14>12, so the strongest is Lens ALens A​ at 215215. Rewriting all three as powers of 2 is what makes them comparable at a glance.
Practice
Collapse this into a single power of 22, exponent and all. (2−3)−4×4−58−18−1(2−3)−4×4−5​
Show the solution
Send every piece to base 22. A power of a power multiplies exponents, so (2−3)−4=2(−3)×(−4)=212.(2−3)−4=2(−3)×(−4)=212. Also 4−5=(22)−5=2−104−5=(22)−5=2−10 and 8−1=(23)−1=2−38−1=(23)−1=2−3. The numerator is 212×2−10=22212×2−10=22, and dividing by 2−32−3 subtracts a negative, which adds. 222−3=22−(−3)=252−322​=22−(−3)=25​ Every minus sign here rides along as an ordinary number, in each law it touches.
